analysis.one_liner: Makes damaging or disrupting an animal-related business a federal crime with penalties up to life.
analysis.headline: Despite 44 cosponsors and a subcommittee hearing, the House never voted on the bill before the 109th Congress ended — and an identical Senate bill was enacted into law in late 2006.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the federal animal-enterprise terrorism law to cover anyone who travels across state lines or uses the mail or internet with the goal of damaging or disrupting a business that uses animals — including farms, furriers, circuses, rodeos, pet stores, and research labs. It sets escalating prison terms based on the financial harm caused, allows restitution for lost profits and the cost of redoing interrupted experiments, and adds the offense to the list of crimes that can be wiretapped. Critics said the broad 'economic disruption' and conspiracy language could sweep in coordinated protest activity.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, businesses that use or sell animals — farms, furriers, zoos, circuses, rodeos, breeders, pet stores, and research laboratories — would gain a federal criminal shield against activists who damage property, cause financial losses, or threaten employees, plus restitution for lost profits and repeated experiments.

how_it_helps.text: Criminalizes traveling in interstate commerce or using the mail or other facilities with the purpose of damaging or disrupting an animal enterprise, including by threats, vandalism, trespass, harassment, or intimidation, with prison terms escalating from 1 year up to life where a death results [S3].
Authorizes restitution for the cost of repeating interrupted experiments, lost farm income, and 'any other economic damage' including losses caused by economic disruption [S2][S3].
Adds the offense to the list of federal crimes for which wiretaps are authorized [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Activists and advocacy groups would face federal felony charges with terrorism-labeled penalties for coordinated protest tactics; defendants would owe restitution that can include a company's lost profits.

drawbacks.text: The bill defines 'animal enterprise' broadly to include pet stores, circuses, rodeos, fairs, and shelters, and defines 'economic disruption' as losses over $10,000 from threats, vandalism, trespass, harassment, or intimidation — language that civil-liberties groups warned could reach coordinated protest and advocacy campaigns, though the bill excludes lawful public reactions to the disclosure of information about an animal enterprise [S3].

Conspiracy and attempt carry the same penalties as the underlying offense, so two people planning disruptive protest could face the same prison terms as someone who carries it out, and any economic damage over $100,000 carries up to 10 years [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Protecting people from genuine threats, vandalism, and violence is legitimate, and the bill's penalty ladder for injury and death tracks ordinary criminal law. The contested part is the expansion to pure 'economic disruption' and conspiracy: financial harm to a company is treated like terrorism with multi-year federal prison terms, and the broad definitions left open the risk that lawful protest coordination could be prosecuted. The bill offered little that existing arson, stalking, and extortion statutes did not already cover, while adding disproportionate penalties for protest-related property crimes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to its Crime subcommittee, got a single subcommittee hearing, and expired when the 109th Congress ended without ever reaching the House floor.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 4, 2005 by Rep. Thomas Petri with 11 original cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S5].
On February 6, 2006 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, which held a hearing on May 23, 2006 [S5].
The committee never reported the bill and the House never voted on it; the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].
The bill had 44 cosponsors — 34 Republicans and 10 Democrats — but no roll-call vote was ever taken in either chamber on this bill [S4].

An identical Senate companion (S. 3880) was passed by the Senate by unanimous consent and signed into law in late 2006, so the substance of this bill became federal law during the same Congress even though this House bill never got a recorded vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: On paper, animal-advocacy groups and civil-liberties critics were spared this bill's penalties because it died in committee — but that is only on paper: an identical bill passed the Senate without a recorded vote and became law in late 2006, so the animal-using industries it was written to protect ultimately got what they sought without any recorded vote on the substance.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Animal enterprises — identical language became law anyway

for.name: Rep. Thomas E. Petri
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor [S1][S5].

against.name: ACLU and civil-liberties organizations
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the Animal Enterprise Terrorism Act, arguing its 'economic disruption' and conspiracy provisions could chill lawful protest and advocacy.

sides.party_line_note: No chamber voted on this bill, but its 44 cosponsors split 34 Republicans to 10 Democrats, showing bipartisan support for the measure.

industries.industry: Animal-using industries (agribusiness, fur trade, rodeos, circuses, breeders)
industries.note: The bill would give these businesses a federal criminal shield against activists, with restitution covering lost profits and farm income. Its effect runs against the public in the sense that the people penalized are protesters exercising political speech, and the law's breadth drew civil-liberties objections.

industries.industry: Animal research laboratories and biomedical testing
industries.note: Laboratories would gain both criminal protection and a novel restitution remedy — the cost of redoing any experiment an activist interrupts. That protects medical research from sabotage, but the same penalties could reach advocacy campaigns aimed at the labs.
